object_description: very small-footprint volume stacking its uses, with the art rooms in the roof structure over the hall
geometry_property: gray wooden cladding with metal window bands
design_condition: the volume is placed along the driveway behind the existing row of trees, parallel to and slightly overlapping the existing hall so the ensemble reads as a unit

positive: The project is characterised by minimal intervention in the existing situation
The new building has a very small footprint
It is aligned parallel to the existing hall so the ensemble reads as a unit
The staggered roof shape creates a volumetric relationship with the existing triple hall
The building maintains a respectful distance from the neighbourhood
The new forecourt connects the two sports hall uses
The arrangement of the bicycle parking makes sense and the parking spaces are functional
The green spaces with seepage troughs, hedges and herbaceous areas could be ecologically very valuable
The small footprint is achieved by stacking the uses
The hall is spanned by two large glued laminated timber trusses
An open and flexible spatial concept is proposed for the three-nave roof structure
The statically determined excess height is cleverly designed as a lantern with skylight strips
The spatial qualities of the open central nave are highly valued
The two side aisles can be freely divided with stud walls and glazed partitions
There are harmonious proportions within the supporting structure
The supporting structure is stringent and carefully designed
The support framework is sensibly placed in the roof level, avoiding sloping supports
The elements are dimensioned plausibly
The stacking of uses is indicated by a horizontal band on the facade
The design draws on the existing campus architecture, with roof and cladding based on the neighbouring hall
The project has good economic viability with a deep floor area and a small building volume
A very small underground volume offsets the complex construction
The system separation is well implemented and the low glazing gives low maintenance costs
A carefully developed and finely balanced project between restraint and independence
The facade materials chosen are durable and low-maintenance
The static concept is convincingly translated into an attractive spatial sequence
negative: Parking directly along the southern border offers potential for conflict
Very large, homogeneous and largely sealed areas result, used primarily for parking
There are no accessible parking spaces at the main entrance
The outside space has little apparent quality of stay and its materialisation is imprecise
The green spaces seem too small in the overall context
Only non-native and large trees are used; more biodiversity and height structure would be desirable
The staircase in the middle of the south facade is spatially and functionally small
The overall entrance situation is rather modest
The external escape staircase seems attached and is not sufficiently dimensioned
Using the central nave as storage or project room conflicts with the open spatial effect
The alternating occupancies are interesting but challenging for school operations
The decentralised access leads to sometimes long and complicated routes
The basement sports facilities are functional but not very inviting
Athletes must walk around the equipment room block to reach the hall
The preparation and staff cloakrooms on the upper floor are operationally unsatisfactory
The large spans lead to large load concentrations with comparatively complex foundations
Space efficiency is partly gained at the expense of more spacious traffic areas
The project turns from pleasantly reserved to overly modest in access and development
The access area hardly offers any quality of stay due to the lack of seating and shade
The design does not do justice to its social function as a meeting place
The exterior design remains very schematic and lacks sensitivity to the neighbourhood
